title: Lesson 11: General Multiplication
subtopics: Revision: multiplying by a single digit from left to right
Moving multiplier for long numbers times two digits
Three-figure extension and pairs of digits
Multiplying binomials with the same pattern
learningGoals: Multiply two-digit, long-by-two-digit, and three-digit numbers using a single coherent vertically-and-crosswise pattern.
Understand how carries are merged in mental left-to-right work and how the same logic appears in written right-to-left work.
Transfer the same multiplication structure from arithmetic into algebraic binomials.
coreIdeas: General multiplication is not a new collection of tricks; it is one expandable pattern of vertical and crosswise products.
Carries are handled by merging adjacent result blocks rather than by restarting the calculation.
The same structure works for digits, grouped digit pairs, and algebraic terms, which makes the method unified and memorable.

workedExamples.method: Compute 56 and 32, then merge the inner carry from 32 into 56 to get 592.
Use left vertical 4, middle crosswise 8, and right vertical 3 to get 483.
Use the moving multiplier to produce 12, 17, 12, 7, and 2, then merge them to 138272.
Use the five-step one-two-three-two-one pattern and merge the results to 161784.

starterPractice: Warm-up: merge the partial products in 74 x 8.
Guided: multiply 23 x 41 by naming left, middle, and right results.
Independent: use the five-step pattern to find 321 x 321.

onboarding.coachIntro: Raj checks language comfort, current confidence, and session goal before starting General Multiplication.
onboarding.placementRule: Recommended start level for Lesson 11: confident. If the learner struggles twice in one step, keep the pace slow and repeat the pattern with a smaller number.

mission.missionPromise: Multiply two-digit, long-by-two-digit, and three-digit numbers using a single coherent vertically-and-crosswise pattern.
mission.successCelebration: Celebrate each correct step in General Multiplication with points, a badge pulse, and a quick coach line before moving on.

microLessonPattern: Coach opens with one short hook and names the pattern.
Coach models one worked move on the board.
Coach reads the exercise question aloud.
Niagh tries before the full answer is shown.
Instant feedback either celebrates or repairs the first mistake.
A quick review prompt decides whether the learner advances or repeats.

rewardLoop.streakRule: Keep the streak visible on every step and protect it with immediate retries instead of long explanations.
rewardLoop.badgeRule: Each exercise group has one badge focus tied to the subtopic being learned.
rewardLoop.celebrationStyle: Short praise, points pulse, and progress-bar movement after every correct response.

reviewLoop.trigger: If the learner answers incorrectly, hesitates, or shows low confidence, reopen the same pattern with one smaller follow-up.
reviewLoop.practiceStyle: Use the micro-practice line as the first repair loop before advancing.
reviewLoop.masteryRule: Advance only after the learner can answer the checkpoint and complete one try in the same subtopic.
reviewLoop.revisitRule: Weak steps should return in the next session as review cards before new content.

uiDirectives.noScrollGoal: The learner should see mission progress, the current question, and the main action buttons without long vertical scrolling.

screenplay.subtopic: Revision: multiplying by a single digit from left to right
screenplay.teacherLine: General multiplication grows out of a smaller left-to-right multiplication idea you already know.
screenplay.boardAction: Write 74 x 8 with space for two partial products.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: Why does seventy-four times eight become five hundred ninety-two when we merge the partial products?
screenplay.fallbackHint: First compute each digit times the single multiplier.

screenplay.subtopic: Revision: multiplying by a single digit from left to right
screenplay.teacherLine: Seven times eight is fifty-six and four times eight is thirty-two.
screenplay.boardAction: Place 56 and 32 side by side on the board.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: Why does seventy-four times eight become five hundred ninety-two when we merge the partial products?
screenplay.fallbackHint: These are not separate answers; they must be merged.

screenplay.subtopic: Revision: multiplying by a single digit from left to right
screenplay.teacherLine: The three in thirty-two carries into the six in fifty-six, so fifty-six comma thirty-two becomes five hundred ninety-two.
screenplay.boardAction: Show 56,32 becoming 592 with the carry marked above.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: Why does seventy-four times eight become five hundred ninety-two when we merge the partial products?
screenplay.fallbackHint: The inner digits merge and the carry moves left.

screenplay.subtopic: Revision: multiplying by a single digit from left to right
screenplay.teacherLine: Now use the same merge on seventy-seven times four.
screenplay.boardAction: Show 28 and 28 as the two partial products.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: Why does seventy-four times eight become five hundred ninety-two when we merge the partial products?
screenplay.fallbackHint: Twenty-eight comma twenty-eight becomes three hundred eight.

screenplay.subtopic: Revision: multiplying by a single digit from left to right
screenplay.teacherLine: Checkpoint: what is the one habit that makes left-to-right single-digit multiplication work?
screenplay.boardAction: Box the phrase compute, then merge.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: Why does seventy-four times eight become five hundred ninety-two when we merge the partial products?
screenplay.expectedStudentResponse: Compute each piece, then merge with carries from right part into left part.
screenplay.fallbackHint: That merging habit returns in the general method.

screenplay.subtopic: Two-figure multiplication vertically and crosswise
screenplay.teacherLine: For two-digit numbers, the multiplication pattern is perfectly symmetric.
screenplay.boardAction: Stack 21 over 23 and label three answer slots.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: How do the three vertically-and-crosswise steps build the full product for a two-digit multiplication?
screenplay.fallbackHint: There are exactly three steps.

screenplay.subtopic: Two-figure multiplication vertically and crosswise
screenplay.teacherLine: Left vertical gives two times two equals four, crosswise gives two times three plus one times two equals eight, and right vertical gives one times three equals three.
screenplay.boardAction: Write 4, then 8, then 3 into the answer slots.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: How do the three vertically-and-crosswise steps build the full product for a two-digit multiplication?
screenplay.fallbackHint: This produces 483.

screenplay.subtopic: Two-figure multiplication vertically and crosswise
screenplay.teacherLine: A carry can happen in the middle step, as in twenty-three times forty-one where the middle total is fourteen.
screenplay.boardAction: Show 2 x 4 = 8, then 2 x 1 + 3 x 4 = 14, then 3 x 1 = 3 and merge to 943.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: How do the three vertically-and-crosswise steps build the full product for a two-digit multiplication?
screenplay.fallbackHint: Carry in the middle is handled by merging leftward.

screenplay.subtopic: Two-figure multiplication vertically and crosswise
screenplay.teacherLine: Now multiply twenty-three by thirty-four using the same pattern.
screenplay.boardAction: Show left 6, middle 17, right 12 on the board.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: How do the three vertically-and-crosswise steps build the full product for a two-digit multiplication?
screenplay.fallbackHint: Merge 6,17,12 from left to right.

screenplay.subtopic: Two-figure multiplication vertically and crosswise
screenplay.teacherLine: Checkpoint: if you forget the order, what phrase brings the whole method back?
screenplay.boardAction: Leave left vertical, crosswise, right vertical in a line.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: How do the three vertically-and-crosswise steps build the full product for a two-digit multiplication?
screenplay.fallbackHint: That phrase is the full two-digit pattern.

screenplay.subtopic: Moving multiplier for long numbers times two digits
screenplay.teacherLine: The same crosswise idea extends to longer numbers by letting the short multiplier move across.
screenplay.boardAction: Write 4321 with 32 first aligned at the left edge.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: Why does the moving multiplier create five partial results for a four-digit number times a two-digit number?
screenplay.fallbackHint: You multiply where the digits overlap.

screenplay.subtopic: Moving multiplier for long numbers times two digits
screenplay.teacherLine: At the far left you get a vertical product, then crosswise products while the 32 slides through the middle, and finally a vertical product at the far right.
screenplay.boardAction: Mark the five positions of 32 under 4321.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: Why does the moving multiplier create five partial results for a four-digit number times a two-digit number?
screenplay.fallbackHint: This gives one result for each overlap position.

screenplay.subtopic: Moving multiplier for long numbers times two digits
screenplay.teacherLine: For 4321 times 32 the five results are 12, 17, 12, 7, and 2, which merge to 138272.
screenplay.boardAction: Write the five results and merge them step by step.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: Why does the moving multiplier create five partial results for a four-digit number times a two-digit number?
screenplay.fallbackHint: Record results in order, then merge.

screenplay.subtopic: Moving multiplier for long numbers times two digits
screenplay.teacherLine: Now list the overlap results for 321 times 21 before giving the final answer.
screenplay.boardAction: Show the aligned positions under 321.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: Why does the moving multiplier create five partial results for a four-digit number times a two-digit number?
screenplay.fallbackHint: The results are 6, 7, 4, 1.

screenplay.subtopic: Moving multiplier for long numbers times two digits
screenplay.teacherLine: Checkpoint: what stays the same between the two-digit pattern and the moving-multiplier pattern?
screenplay.boardAction: Box the words vertical at ends, crosswise in middle.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: Why does the moving multiplier create five partial results for a four-digit number times a two-digit number?
screenplay.expectedStudentResponse: The ends are vertical and the middle positions are crosswise.
screenplay.fallbackHint: Only the number of middle steps changes.

screenplay.subtopic: Three-figure extension and pairs of digits
screenplay.teacherLine: Three-figure multiplication is still one pattern, only stretched symmetrically.
screenplay.boardAction: Stack 504 over 321 and mark five answer stages A to E.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: How does the one-two-three-two-one pattern organize a full three-digit multiplication?
screenplay.fallbackHint: The step counts go one, two, three, two, one.

screenplay.subtopic: Three-figure extension and pairs of digits
screenplay.teacherLine: For 504 times 321 the five totals are fifteen, ten, seventeen, eight, and four, which merge to 161784.
screenplay.boardAction: Write each stage under the diagram and merge after each step.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: How does the one-two-three-two-one pattern organize a full three-digit multiplication?
screenplay.fallbackHint: The middle stage uses three products.

screenplay.subtopic: Three-figure extension and pairs of digits
screenplay.teacherLine: If you split numbers into groups, like 3 slash 04 and 4 slash 12, the same pattern returns but now the answer appears in two-digit blocks.
screenplay.boardAction: Write 304 x 412 as 3/04 x 4/12 and compute 12, 52, 48.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: How does the one-two-three-two-one pattern organize a full three-digit multiplication?
screenplay.fallbackHint: Grouped digits preserve the same symmetry.

screenplay.subtopic: Three-figure extension and pairs of digits
screenplay.teacherLine: Now square 321 by the five-step pattern.
screenplay.boardAction: Show 321 over 321 with blank stage totals.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: How does the one-two-three-two-one pattern organize a full three-digit multiplication?
screenplay.fallbackHint: The stage totals are 9, 12, 10, 4, and 1.

screenplay.subtopic: Three-figure extension and pairs of digits
screenplay.teacherLine: Checkpoint: why is the middle step of a three-digit product the busiest one?
screenplay.boardAction: Underline the three-product middle band in the diagram.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: How does the one-two-three-two-one pattern organize a full three-digit multiplication?
screenplay.expectedStudentResponse: Because it combines hundreds-by-units, tens-by-tens, and units-by-hundreds.
screenplay.fallbackHint: That is the center of the symmetry.

screenplay.subtopic: Multiplying binomials with the same pattern
screenplay.teacherLine: Vedic multiplication does not split arithmetic and algebra into separate methods.
screenplay.boardAction: Stack x + 3 over x + 4 in the same layout as a two-digit product.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: Why does the exact same multiplication pattern work for binomials and for two-digit numbers?
screenplay.fallbackHint: The pattern is structural, not tied to digits only.

screenplay.subtopic: Multiplying binomials with the same pattern
screenplay.teacherLine: Left vertical gives x squared, crosswise gives four x plus three x, and right vertical gives twelve.
screenplay.boardAction: Write x^2, 7x, and 12 into the result slots.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: Why does the exact same multiplication pattern work for binomials and for two-digit numbers?
screenplay.fallbackHint: So the product is x squared plus seven x plus twelve.

screenplay.subtopic: Multiplying binomials with the same pattern
screenplay.teacherLine: Negative terms fit too: two x minus three times three x plus four gives six x squared, minus x, and minus twelve.
screenplay.boardAction: Show 2x x 3x, then 8x minus 9x, then minus 12.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: Why does the exact same multiplication pattern work for binomials and for two-digit numbers?
screenplay.fallbackHint: Crosswise terms are simply added with their signs.

screenplay.subtopic: Multiplying binomials with the same pattern
screenplay.teacherLine: Now expand x plus five times x plus six with the same three-step pattern.
screenplay.boardAction: Show left, middle, right slots as blanks.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: Why does the exact same multiplication pattern work for binomials and for two-digit numbers?
screenplay.fallbackHint: Left x^2, middle 11x, right 30.

screenplay.subtopic: Multiplying binomials with the same pattern
screenplay.teacherLine: Checkpoint: what is the only new thing you must watch in algebra compared with arithmetic?
screenplay.boardAction: Leave signs highlighted in the crosswise term.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: Why does the exact same multiplication pattern work for binomials and for two-digit numbers?
screenplay.expectedStudentResponse: The signs of the terms when combining the crosswise part.
screenplay.fallbackHint: The structure stays the same.

screenplay.subtopic: Written right-to-left calculations
screenplay.teacherLine: Written calculation is the same method viewed from the opposite end.
screenplay.boardAction: Write 42 over 31 and put the answer line underneath.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: How does the written right-to-left form match the mental pattern instead of replacing it?
screenplay.fallbackHint: You begin at the rightmost vertical step.

screenplay.subtopic: Written right-to-left calculations
screenplay.teacherLine: For forty-two times thirty-one, two times one gives two, then crosswise gives ten, so write zero and carry one, then left vertical gives thirteen.
screenplay.boardAction: Write the answer 1302 with the carries above the columns.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: How does the written right-to-left form match the mental pattern instead of replacing it?
screenplay.fallbackHint: Each written step matches one mental step.

screenplay.subtopic: Written right-to-left calculations
screenplay.teacherLine: The same approach scales to long products like 4321 times 24 and 234 times 234.
screenplay.boardAction: Show the right-to-left steps for 86 x 23 and indicate where each carry is written.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: How does the written right-to-left form match the mental pattern instead of replacing it?
screenplay.fallbackHint: You are still doing vertical and crosswise operations in order.

screenplay.subtopic: Written right-to-left calculations
screenplay.teacherLine: Now write out thirty-one times forty-one from right to left.
screenplay.boardAction: Show a blank answer line and the first rightmost step.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: How does the written right-to-left form match the mental pattern instead of replacing it?
screenplay.fallbackHint: Right vertical first, then crosswise, then left vertical.

screenplay.subtopic: Written right-to-left calculations
screenplay.teacherLine: Final checkpoint: when might you prefer the written version over the mental version?
screenplay.boardAction: Leave mental and written as two boxes on the board.
screenplay.checkpointPrompt: How does the written right-to-left form match the mental pattern instead of replacing it?
screenplay.expectedStudentResponse: When the carries are too many to hold mentally or the numbers are longer.
screenplay.fallbackHint: The rule is the same; only the support changes.

teachingFlowStages.intent: Introduce general multiplication as one scalable pattern rather than a set of unrelated cases.
Explain left-to-right merging, vertical-crosswise order, and the growing symmetry of longer products.
Demonstrate two-digit, moving-multiplier, three-digit, and algebraic examples on the board.
Have the learner say the stage totals first and then assemble the final answer.
Mix easy, carry, long-number, and written forms so the student uses the same logic in different settings.
Check carries, stage order, and final merging to keep the long calculations reliable.
Require the learner to explain why the arithmetic and algebraic versions are really the same method.
